title: The seal audit — every seal that exists in validation/ verifies
checksList: ok: A1: the namespace scan visited records
ok: A1: the scan found sealed records to verify (a walker that reads nothing cannot pass)
ok: A2: every sealed record's bbSeal verifies (no stale seal anywhere in validation/)
ok: A2: no sealed record carries a malformed bbSeal envelope
ok: A2: no record claiming a seal is unparseable (an unverifiable seal is a refusal, not a pass)
ok: A3: every seal verdict agrees with the library's trusted read
ok: A3: the agreement check compared every sealed record
ok: A4: every register row names a file whose seal still equals the refreshed digest
ok: A4: every register row carries a written reason
ok: A5: the scan found a valid sealed record to use as the proof's baseline
ok: A5: a sealed record's untouched copy reads valid
ok: A5: the same record with content added after sealing reads STALE
ok: A5: the audit's stale verdict is not a constant (the untouched copy passed the same run above) [negative]
ok: A5: a record with its seal stripped reads unsealed (not valid, not stale)
ok: A5: a malformed envelope reads bad-envelope
limitations: The audit covers the `validation/` evidence namespace (where milestone records live) and says nothing about sealed records stored elsewhere; no other directory was measured.

Its claim is that every seal that EXISTS verifies — not that every record is sealed. The unsealed population is measured and recorded in `data` (with the unparseable records, which are the JSON analyzer's deliberately-invalid fixtures), and sealing the rest is the M61 D-1 migration's own unfinished work, not this gate's.
A seal verifies INTEGRITY (the record is exactly what its writer sealed), not freshness or truth: a stale-DATA record with a valid seal passes here by design.
A5's can-fail proof uses copies of a real sealed record in a temp dir; the classification of the real namespace is the same code path run once, read-only, so no real artifact is written by the audit.
